title: Mutable vs immutable types
body: Immutable objects cannot change after creation: int, float, bool, str, tuple and frozenset. Operations on them create new objects. Mutable objects can change in place: list, dict, set and most user-defined objects. Assignment never copies; it binds another name to the same object, so b = a followed by b.append(4) also changes a. Use a[:], list(a) or copy.copy() for a shallow copy, and copy.deepcopy() when nested objects must be copied too. Only hashable (typically immutable) objects can be dict keys or set elements, which is why a list cannot be a dict key.
example:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
c = a.copy()
b.append(3)
print(a, c)       # [1, 2, 3] [1, 2]
print(a is b)     # True
interview_tip: Explain the difference between == (equal values) and is (same object), and why a tuple holding a list can still change.

title: Scope: the LEGB rule, global and nonlocal
body: Python looks up a name in four scopes, in order: Local, Enclosing function, Global (module) and Built-in. Any assignment to a name inside a function makes that name local to the whole function, so reading it before the assignment raises UnboundLocalError. Declare global name to assign to a module-level variable, or nonlocal name to assign to a variable in the nearest enclosing function. Reading an outer variable needs no declaration; only rebinding it does. Inner functions that use enclosing variables form closures, which keep those variables alive after the outer function returns.
example:
def make_counter():
    n = 0
    def step():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
        return n
    return step

c = make_counter()
c()
print(c())   # 2
interview_tip: If asked why count += 1 fails inside a function, say that the assignment makes count local, so Python never looks at the global.

title: List, dict and set comprehensions
body: A comprehension builds a collection in one expression: [expr for x in iterable if condition]. Use {k: v for ...} for a dict and {expr for ...} for a set. Several for clauses nest from left to right, exactly like nested loops written in the same order. Parentheses instead of brackets create a generator expression, which produces values lazily and can be consumed only once; it saves memory for large data, for example sum(x * x for x in range(10**6)). Comprehensions have their own scope, so the loop variable does not leak. Keep them short; use a normal loop when logic gets complex.
interview_tip: Be ready to rewrite a nested loop as a comprehension and to explain when a generator expression is the better choice.

title: Function arguments: defaults, *args and **kwargs
body: Parameters can be positional, keyword, or have default values. Defaults are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, so a mutable default such as [] is shared by every call; use None and create the list inside the function. *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. In a call, * unpacks a sequence and ** unpacks a dict into arguments. Python passes object references: a function can mutate a list it receives, but rebinding the parameter name does not affect the caller.
interview_tip: The mutable default argument bug is a favourite question; show the def f(x, items=None) fix.

title: Core built-in types and their traps
body: list is ordered and mutable; tuple is ordered and immutable; set holds unique, unordered, hashable items; dict maps unique keys to values and keeps insertion order (guaranteed since Python 3.7). / always returns a float and // floors, so -7 // 2 is -4. round() uses round-half-to-even, so round(2.5) is 2. Floating-point values are binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is False; compare with math.isclose(). A one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,). Empty containers, 0, None and "" are falsy; every non-empty string, including "False", is truthy.
example:
import math
print(-7 // 2, round(2.5), (5,) == (5))   # -4 2 False
print(math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))        # True
interview_tip: Choose the right type out loud: a set for fast membership tests, a dict for lookups by key, a tuple for fixed records.
